sections.section: The objects of the chapter and the running case
sections.lecture_material: Room of size L (cube root of the volume), temperature theta at about 300 K, heat diffusivity (slides gamma), r.m.s. velocity u.
sections.research_extension: U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976: eqs. (51), (53) (p. 19), Table 10 (p. 20), ratio of specific heats 1.40 (p. 18); nu = 1.57e-5 m^2/s, Gamma = 2.22e-5 m^2/s, Pr = 0.71 at 300 K.
sections.teaching_construction: Formal model of the room and its three times; meaning of ~; note on gamma as a diffusivity.

sections.section: Turbulence begins as an instability of a laminar flow
sections.lecture_material: Turbulence arises from instabilities of laminar flow; pipe Re = UD/nu ~ 2100 (roughness makes transition sooner); zero-pressure-gradient boundary layer unstable at U delta*/nu ~ 600; critical Reynolds number.
sections.research_extension: Reynolds 1883 (pp. 943, 946, 948): sensitivity to inlet disturbance, two critical velocities, ratio 278/43.79. Meseguer and Trefethen 2003 (preprint pp. 1, 4, 10-11, 15-16): decaying eigenmodes to R = 1e7, transition depends on nonlinearity, transition near 2000. Schubauer and Skramstad 1948 (pp. 2, 7, 30): instability versus transition, delta* = 1.72 (nu x/U0)^(1/2), lower limit 450, transition at R_x ~ 2.8e6 and 1.5e6 by free-stream turbulence.
sections.teaching_construction: Definitions (4.1); conversion (4.2) of Re_delta* to Re_x; statement that each critical Re belongs to one flow, one length and one disturbance level.

sections.section: Free shear layers can be unstable without viscosity
sections.lecture_material: Free shear flows unstable at very low Re by an inviscid mechanism that does not operate in boundary layers and pipe flow; wall flows have a velocity gradient because of the surface.
sections.research_extension: Darrigol 2002 (pp. 49-50): Rayleigh's 1880 stability equation and inflection-point criterion, eq. (19) vorticity conservation. Blasius 1908 (TM p. 7): zeta zeta'' = -zeta'''. Meseguer and Trefethen 2003 (p. 15): plane Poiseuille eigenvalue instability at R ~ 5772. Schubauer and Skramstad (pp. 1, 30): viscous stability theory of Tollmien and Schlichting, 'good agreement with theory'.
sections.teaching_construction: In-place proof that 2D inviscid vorticity is conserved (curl of the inviscid momentum equation; stretching term zero in 2D); derivation (4.3)-(4.5) in book notation; three-profile check (tanh, Poiseuille, Blasius sign argument); boundary (necessary, inviscid, linear, parallel).

sections.section: Turbulence needs a supply of energy
sections.lecture_material: Turbulence cannot maintain itself; it depends on its environment for energy; shear and buoyancy as common sources.
sections.research_extension: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Room as buoyancy source.

sections.section: Turbulence begins as an instability of a laminar flow (flat-plate figure, treated in that section)
sections.lecture_material: Figure of a flat-plate boundary layer: laminar region, transition region, turbulent region; low and high mixing; fuller turbulent profile.
sections.research_extension: Schubauer and Skramstad 1948 (pp. 2, 7, 30) for the positions of instability and transition.
sections.teaching_construction: The du/dy labels rendered as a statement about the wall gradient; the figure placed with the Re_delta* to Re_x conversion.

sections.section: Turbulence needs a supply of energy (continued)
sections.lecture_material: Turbulence decays without shear or buoyancy; Re decreases and the flow tends to laminar; decay of grid turbulence; Taylor's hypothesis recalled; laminarization by magnetic fields and stable stratification.
sections.research_extension: None.

sections.section: Turbulence begins as an instability of a laminar flow (from instability to developed turbulence, treated in that section)

sections.section: Without air motion, heat crosses the room in days
sections.lecture_material: Diffusivity as the outstanding characteristic; orders of magnitude faster transfer (fire versus candle flame); imposed-length problem; heat equation (slide eq. 1); Tm ~ L^2/gamma (slide eq. 2); L = 5 m gives order 1e6 s, more than 100 h.
sections.research_extension: Gamma at 300 K from the Standard Atmosphere formulas.
sections.teaching_construction: Numerical value 1.1e6 s; slowest-mode exact solution in an insulated cube, tau_1 = L^2/(pi^2 Gamma) = 32 h; 10 % time 73 h; dependence of the constant on the definition.

sections.section: A weak buoyant stir mixes the room in minutes
sections.lecture_material: Weak buoyant motions disperse heat quickly; Tt ~ L/u (slide eq. 3); buoyant acceleration g dtheta/theta ~ 0.3 m/s^2; KE g h dtheta/theta ~ 0.03 m^2/s^2; 17 cm/s; u ~ 5 cm/s; Tt = 100 s; eddies of about 1 cm smoothed in l^2/gamma, a few seconds.
sections.research_extension: None.
sections.teaching_construction: sqrt(2) discrepancy between the slide speed and (1/2)V^2; ratio Tm/Tt = 1.1e4 with uncertainty; two-step mechanism (transport by large eddies, molecular smoothing at 1 cm, 4.5 s).

sections.section: A weak buoyant stir mixes the room in minutes (recap)
sections.lecture_material: Recap of the room case: 100 hours versus 2 minutes; 1 cm eddies dissipated in a few seconds; diffusion by random motion very rapid.
sections.research_extension: As above.
sections.teaching_construction: As above.

sections.section: The ratio of the two times is a Peclet number
sections.lecture_material: Tt/Tm ~ gamma/(uL) = 1/Pe (slide eq. 4); for gases gamma ~ nu, nu/gamma = 0.73 = Pr, so Tt/Tm ~ 1/Re (slide eq. 5); larger Re widens the gap.
sections.research_extension: Pr = 0.71 at 300 K (Standard Atmosphere formulas).
sections.teaching_construction: Identity Pe = Pr Re; room values Pe = 1.1e4, Re = 1.6e4; domain limit at Pe ~ 1 (Exercise 1).

sections.section: The ratio of the two times is a Peclet number (Re as a ratio of times)
sections.lecture_material: Re = 15000 in the example; Re as ratio of a turbulence time to a molecular time; Tennekes and Lumley: more reliable than inertia/viscous ratio because viscous effects act at smaller scales than inertia effects.
sections.research_extension: None.
sections.teaching_construction: L^2/nu over L/u = Re; the lecture's argument stated as the lecture's reasoning; the judgement attributed, not adopted.

sections.section: The eddy diffusivity
sections.lecture_material: Effective diffusivity K (slide eq. 6); turbulence treated as a fluid property, conceptually dangerous; hypothetical turbulent diffusion process; T ~ L^2/K = Tt gives K ~ uL (slide eqs. 7-8); K/gamma ~ K/nu ~ Re (slide eq. 9); recap of the whole argument.
sections.research_extension: None.
sections.teaching_construction: K = 0.25 m^2/s for the room; calibration-not-prediction statement.

sections.lecture_material: None (motivated by the lecture's 'hypothetical turbulent diffusion process').
sections.research_extension: Taylor 1922 (read 1920): p. 196 quotation; p. 197 heat flux -rho sigma beta [u(x-a)] and [uX] = (1/2) d[X^2]/dt; p. 207 eq. (18) and short-time eq. (19); p. 208 eq. (20) long-time limit with finite integral I.
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of the flux -rho c_p beta <u_p X> from the initial linear temperature and of <u_p X> = (1/2) d<X^2>/dt; derivation of (4.15) through <u_p X> = u^2 int R_L ds with stationarity (R_L depends on the time difference and is even) stated; K(t) = (1/2) d<X^2>/dt from the flux comparison; K = u^2 T_L; exponential-correlation example (4.17) with values at T_L and 10 T_L; Figure 4.1; application to the room (T_L ~ L/u, 10 T_L ~ 1000 s, walls).

sections.section: The objects of the chapter and the running case

sections.section: An imposed time scale fixes the depth of the atmospheric boundary layer
sections.lecture_material: Coriolis parameter and imposed time 1/f; laminar estimate L_m^2 ~ nu T = 40 cm; eddy diffusivity K ~ uL; L_t ~ uT = 3 km; L_t = u/(4f) correlation; large eddies comparable to flow width.
sections.research_extension: AMS Glossary: f = 2 Omega sin(latitude), Omega = 7.2921e-5 rad/s; f = 9.4e-5 1/s at 40 degrees.
sections.teaching_construction: Hinge that K grows with depth (T^1 versus T^(1/2)); dimensional reading u/f; buoyancy boundary.

sections.section: The ratio of the two depths is the square root of a Reynolds number
sections.lecture_material: L_t/L_m ~ (u^2/(f nu))^(1/2) = Re^(1/2); imposed-length case Re ~ T_m/T_t; Pr of air 0.73; turbulence a more effective diffusion agent.
sections.research_extension: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Numerical check 6e7 and 7.7e3 against the direct ratio; explanation of first power versus square root.

sections.section: Inertia and viscosity act at different lengths
sections.lecture_material: Range of scales bounded by flow size and viscosity; steady Navier-Stokes scale estimates U^2/L and nu U/L^2; ratio Re; no-slip prevents neglecting viscosity.
sections.research_extension: Blasius 1908 (NACA TM 1256, p. 3): friction gains influence when the friction constant is of order the squared thickness.
sections.teaching_construction: Singular-perturbation explanation; exactly solvable advection-diffusion model problem (5.7); fetch construction showing the viscous length after fetch UT equals L_m.

sections.section: Inertia and viscosity act at different lengths (continued)
sections.lecture_material: Viscous length l chosen so that viscous and inertial terms balance; l/L ~ Re^(-1/2).
sections.research_extension: As above.
sections.teaching_construction: Explanation of the exponent -1/2 versus -1 by the directions of the two derivatives.

sections.section: Diffusive and convective lengths in laminar and turbulent boundary layers
sections.lecture_material: Transverse diffusive length and convective length; slender shear flows; Prandtl approximation l/L -> 0; turbulent dl/dt ~ u, t ~ L/U, l/L ~ u/U; laminar l ~ (nu t)^(1/2); relations are not spreading-rate formulas.
sections.research_extension: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Crossover Re = (U/u)^2; running-case fetch U/f reproducing u/f, with the statement that this is bookkeeping, not confirmation.

sections.section: Skin friction: why the turbulent drag coefficient is larger
sections.lecture_material: D ~ rho U^2 l, C_d ~ 2 Re^(-1/2) laminar; D ~ rho u U l, C_d ~ 2 (u/U)^2 turbulent; turbulence level varies slowly with Re; drag-coefficient figure with transition sensitivity.
sections.research_extension: Blasius 1908 (NACA TM 1256, p. 18): two-sided drag 1.327 b (mu rho l U^3)^(1/2), giving C_d = 1.327 Re^(-1/2) per side.
sections.teaching_construction: Wall-stress consistency checks (laminar tau_w ~ mu U/l; turbulent tau_w ~ rho u^2, u as friction velocity); Table 5.1; crossover Reynolds numbers; factor-9 sensitivity to u/U.

sections.section: Viscosity cannot be removed: the small scales
sections.lecture_material: Large eddies do the transport; nonlinear generation of small scales; viscosity prevents infinitely small scales; singular small parameter; two-bin simplification; small time scales imply supply approximately equals dissipation and statistical independence; universal equilibrium theory.
sections.research_extension: Kolmogorov 1941 (p. 10 footnote): cascade of pulsations until the Reynolds number of order n is small; energy of finest pulsations becomes heat. Definition of the dissipation rate (p. 12, eq. 14).
sections.teaching_construction: Definition of epsilon with units before use; three-step argument with hypothesis labels; comparison with the wall-forced laminar layer.

sections.section: The Kolmogorov scales follow from the dimensions of the dissipation rate and the viscosity
sections.lecture_material: eta = (nu^3/eps)^(1/4), tau = (nu/eps)^(1/2), v = (nu eps)^(1/4) by Buckingham pi; Re formed with eta and v equals one; small-scale motion quite viscous.
sections.research_extension: Kolmogorov 1941 (p. 12, eqs. 15-20): the scales and the unit-viscosity, unit-dissipation rescaling.
sections.teaching_construction: Exponent equations with determinant; uniqueness statement; Re_eta = 1 shown as identity with the physical claim separated; notation change tau, v -> tau_eta, u_eta; sensitivity to epsilon.

sections.lecture_material: Recap of the scales and of the unit Reynolds number.

sections.section: An inviscid estimate of the dissipation rate
sections.lecture_material: Energy u^2, transfer rate u/l, eps ~ u^3/l; dissipation passive; significant energy fraction lost per turnover l/u; viscous decay time l^2/nu and rate nu u^2/l^2.
sections.research_extension: McComb, Berera, Yoffe, Linkmann 2015: C_eps = C_eps,inf + C'/R_L, C_eps,inf = 0.468 +/- 0.006, C' = 18.9 +/- 1.3 for forced isotropic DNS up to R_L = 5875; other studies about 0.4 and 0.5; energy balance with inertial and viscous terms of the same forms. Standard definition of the integral length scale given with a pointer to chapter 8.
sections.teaching_construction: Ratio of viscous to inertial loss = 1/Re_l; running-case times (56 min, 2100 years) and epsilon = 2.7e-5 m^2/s^3 with its scope limit.

sections.section: The scale ratios widen as the Reynolds number increases
sections.lecture_material: eta/l ~ Re^(-3/4), tau u/l ~ Re^(-1/2), v/u ~ Re^(-1/4); separation widens with Re; statistical independence most evident at large Re; two jets at different Re with the same nozzle.
sections.research_extension: Constant-dependence of the ratios using the measured C_eps.
sections.teaching_construction: Ratios with C_eps kept; running-case values; Figure 5.1 (computed log-axis ladder); consistency-not-proof remark on the time-scale assumption.

sections.section: Energy is carried by large scales and vorticity by small scales
sections.lecture_material: Vorticity has units 1/s and scales as reciprocal time; small-scale vorticity much larger; small-scale energy much smaller; most energy at large scales, most vorticity at small scales.
sections.research_extension: Kolmogorov 1941 (pp. 11-12, eqs. 11 and 14): eps = 15 nu <(du1/dx1)^2> under local isotropy, so the rms velocity gradient is 1/(15^(1/2) tau_eta).
sections.teaching_construction: Ratios Re^(1/2) and Re^(-1/2) with running-case numbers.

sections.section: A resolution budget for a direct simulation
sections.lecture_material: DNS grid size comparable to the Kolmogorov length as the first check; eta estimated from Re before a simulation.
sections.research_extension: Yeung, Sreenivasan, Pope 2018 (p. 064603-3): dx/eta ~ 2.96/(k_max eta), k_max eta ~ 1.5 adequate for low-order statistics, larger for higher-order statistics because of intermittency; Courant constraint with beta ~ 12. Pope 2004 (pp. 4, 5, 6): cost factor 16 per halving; CPU time 16 and memory 8 per halving; requirements grow as a power of Re; near-wall viscous region.
sections.teaching_construction: N ~ Re^(3/4), N^3 ~ Re^(9/4), work ~ Re^3; running-case grid 3.5e15 points.

sections.section: The continuum hypothesis and the two descriptions of a flow

sections.section: Conservation of mass and the incompressible approximation
sections.lecture_material: Continuity equation (slide eq. 1); material and specific-volume forms (slide eq. 2); incompressible flow gives div U = 0 (solenoidal); incompressibility defined as density independent of pressure.

sections.section: Momentum, the Newtonian stress and the Navier-Stokes equations
sections.lecture_material: Newton's second law; surface and body forces; symmetric stress tensor; momentum equation (slide eq. 3); Newtonian stress split into isotropic and deviatoric parts (slide eq. 4).
sections.research_extension: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Trace of the viscous stress is 2 mu div U (deviatoric only when div U = 0).

sections.section: Momentum, the Newtonian stress and the Navier-Stokes equations (continued)
sections.lecture_material: Substitution of the stress into the momentum equation using continuity; incompressible Navier-Stokes equations (slide eq. 5); impermeability and no-slip conditions; Euler equations; Euler solutions differ from vanishing-viscosity NS solutions; Euler equations still used.
sections.research_extension: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Index derivation showing where continuity enters; four equations for four unknowns; backward link to chapter 5's singular-perturbation section.

sections.section: Pressure is fixed by the constraint of zero divergence
sections.lecture_material: Pressure acts like a body force with no connection to density; four equations, four unknowns, no pressure equation; divergence of momentum gives the Poisson equation (slide eq. 6); Poisson equation necessary and sufficient for a solenoidal field to remain solenoidal; solution procedure (assume p, correct by Poisson).
sections.research_extension: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Evolution equation for div U (6.11) and the necessity/sufficiency argument with its two conditions; wall Neumann condition (6.13); free-space Green's-function solution and non-locality (6.14); magnitude p ~ rho u0^2 = 4.9 Pa. Uniqueness in the sufficiency argument taken from the maximum principle (6.16) with Gamma = nu.

sections.section: Conserved passive scalars and their bounds
sections.lecture_material: Conserved passive scalar equation (slide eq. 7); temperature and mixture fraction, thermal and mass diffusivity; boundedness phi_min <= phi <= phi_max; passive (temperature) versus active (reacting species) in the lecture's usage; summary of the equation set.
sections.research_extension: None.

sections.section: The vorticity equation and vortex stretching
sections.lecture_material: Vorticity as curl of U (slide eq. 8); turbulence is rotational; curl of NS with the vector identity for the convective term (slide eq. 9); pressure term vanishes; vortex stretching stretches material lines aligned with omega; stretching vanishes in 2D; 2D turbulence vastly different from 3D (slide).
sections.research_extension: Boffetta and Ecke 2012: 2D turbulence never strictly realized but approximates large-scale atmosphere and oceans (p. 428); enstrophy bound dZ/dt = -2 nu P, energy dissipation vanishes as nu -> 0, inverse energy cascade, contrast with 3D vortex stretching (p. 430).
sections.teaching_construction: Baroclinic term shown to vanish only for constant density; material-line equation (6.19) and the Cauchy-type correspondence for nu = 0; enstrophy equation (6.20); 2D enstrophy bound (6.21) derived; running-case vorticity ratio 117.

sections.section: Rates of strain and rotation
sections.lecture_material: Decomposition of the velocity gradient (slide eq. 10); S_ij and Omega_ij (slide eqs. 11-12); tau_ij = -p delta_ij + 2 mu S_ij, viscous stress independent of rotation; omega_i = -eps_ijk Omega_jk (slide eq. 13); Omega_ij a tensor, omega_i not.
sections.research_extension: Hunt, Wray and Moin 1988 (p. 196, eqs. 2.1-2.2): II = du_i/dx_j du_j/dx_i = E_ij^2 - omega_i^2/2; eddy zones where II < -II_E, plus a pressure-minimum criterion.
sections.teaching_construction: Sign check of (6.24) and its inverse; pseudovector argument with det(a); (omega.grad)U = S omega and the stretching/tilting split; Poisson right side as S:S - |omega|^2/2 (6.26) with rigid-rotation and plane-strain limit checks; box-average balance (6.27) and eps = nu <omega'^2> for homogeneous fluctuations; running-case rms vorticity 2.3e3 1/s.
